title: In the Cistern, and a Last Offer to the King
summary: Four officials demand Jeremiah's death because his call to surrender is breaking the city's morale, and Zedekiah lets them lower him into a muddy cistern. Ebed-melech, a Cushite official of the palace, persuades the king to rescue him. Zedekiah then meets Jeremiah in secret, hears once more that surrender means life and resistance means fire, and cannot bring himself to act.
story: The siege has resumed after the Egyptian army withdrew (37:5-11), food is running out, and the argument inside Jerusalem is now open. Jeremiah's message has not changed since chapter 21: the city will fall, and those who go out to the Babylonians will live. To the war party this is defeatism. The chapter brings Jeremiah nearer to death than at any point in the book, then shows God's rescue coming through an unlikely outsider. It ends with the book's last private conversation between prophet and king, the final opportunity Zedekiah has to spare the city. Chapter 39 tells what came of his refusal.
historical:
The siege lasted from about January 588 BC to the summer of 587 or 586 BC (the exact year depends on how the reigns are counted, and scholars divide on it). By this stage, famine was severe (verse 9; 52:6). Several of the officials named in verse 1 appear elsewhere: Pashhur son of Malchijah had earlier been sent to Jeremiah by the king (21:1), and Jucal (Jehucal) son of Shelemiah was one of the king's envoys in 37:3. A clay bulla reading Gedaliah son of Pashhur was found in the City of David by Eilat Mazar in 2008, near the spot where the Jehucal bulla had been found in 2005, and many scholars think these belonged to the officials named here, though this can't be proven.

The officials' complaint in verse 4 is that Jeremiah is weakening the hands of the soldiers, which is the Hebrew idiom behind the BSB's "discouraging". One of the Lachish letters, the military dispatches from these same months found at Lachish in 1935, uses a very similar expression, complaining that certain words from officials in Jerusalem were weakening the hands of the people. The letter doesn't name Jeremiah, and the connection is one of shared language, but it shows that morale and defeatist talk were live concerns in Judah's last days.
cultural:
Cisterns were bell-shaped chambers cut into limestone to catch winter rain, with a narrow opening at the top. A dry cistern made a convenient prison or grave, as in Joseph's story (Genesis 37:24). By the end of a long siege, the water was gone and only mud remained. A person left there without food would die slowly, and a starving man would be unable to climb out. Ebed-melech's rags and worn clothes (verses 11 and 12) are a small act of practical care: padding so the ropes would not cut the prisoner's armpits as thirty men hauled him up.

Ebed-melech's name means servant of the king, which may be a title as much as a name. He is called a Cushite, a man from Cush, the land south of Egypt along the upper Nile (roughly modern Sudan). The word describing his office often means a court official and sometimes specifically a eunuch; it's not certain which sense applies here. That a foreigner of this kind is the only person at court to speak for the prophet is part of the chapter's point. The king's sitting in the Gate of Benjamin (verse 7) reflects the city gate as the place where kings and elders heard petitions and gave judgment.
literary: The chapter has two scenes of about equal length, each ending with the refrain that Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard (verses 13 and 28). In the first, the king says to the officials, "He is in your hands" (verse 5), a confession of weakness from a man who is supposed to rule. In the second, the same king swears secret oaths and fears being mocked. Jeremiah's words to Zedekiah are built as balanced alternatives: if you surrender, you live; if you don't, the city burns (verses 17 and 18). The song of the palace women in verse 22 turns the image of the cistern back on the king: Jeremiah sank in the mud, and now the women sing that Zedekiah's own "feet sank into the mire". The chapter ends not with a decision but with the king's cover story, which says everything about the man.

outline.t: The officials demand Jeremiah's death and drop him into a cistern
A secret meeting: surrender and live
The king's cover story and Jeremiah's confinement

doctrines.note: God keeps his promise to protect Jeremiah (1:19) not by a miracle but through the courage of one foreign official and a bundle of old rags.
Zedekiah believes Jeremiah enough to consult him in secret but not enough to obey. The chapter shows the difference between agreeing that God has spoken and trusting him enough to act.
An outsider from Cush is the one who acts justly when Judah's own leaders do not, a pattern the Old Testament repeats in figures like Rahab and Ruth and that anticipates the inclusion of the nations.

words.note: Bor, pit or cistern. The same word names the dungeon of 37:16 and the cistern of verse 6. In the Psalms the pit often stands for death and the grave (for example Psalm 40:2), so being lifted out of the bor carries the sense of being brought back from death.

Yatsa, to go out, here in the sense of going out to surrender. The ordinary verb for leaving takes on a hard meaning in the siege: to walk out of the gate to the enemy. Jeremiah's offer in verse 17 turns on it: go out and live.
Chayah, to live. It recurs throughout the chapter (verses 2, 17, 20). Jeremiah's message is framed as a choice between life and death, echoing the covenant choice of Deuteronomy 30:15-20.

Shalom, here well-being. The officials accuse Jeremiah of not seeking the shalom of the people (verse 4). Ironically, his whole counsel was aimed at their survival, and in 29:7 he had told the exiles to seek the shalom of Babylon.

christ: The Gospels and early Christians read the pattern of the righteous sufferer who is thrown into the pit and raised out of it as fulfilled in Jesus, especially through the Psalms of lament that use the same imagery. Jeremiah is not a direct prophecy of Christ here, but his story belongs to that pattern: a messenger of God, handed over by a weak ruler to those who want him dead, who descends into the pit and is brought up again. The difference is instructive. Jeremiah is rescued before death; Jesus went all the way into death and was raised. And the life Jeremiah offers the city through surrender anticipates the gospel's paradox, that life is found by giving up the effort to save oneself.

hard.q: Wasn't Jeremiah guilty of treason, telling soldiers and citizens to surrender to the enemy during a war?
hard.a: From the officials' point of view the charge was reasonable, and many modern readers feel its force: no city under siege tolerates a public voice urging defection. Jeremiah's defenders make three points. First, he did not act for Babylon's sake but spoke what he understood as God's verdict on Judah's covenant unfaithfulness; his loyalty was to God, not to either empire. Second, Zedekiah himself had sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar in God's name (2 Chronicles 36:13; Ezekiel 17:13-19), so rebellion was itself a broken oath. Third, Jeremiah's counsel was aimed at saving lives, and the city's fall proved him right. Readers still differ on how far Jeremiah's stance can serve as a model for dissent in wartime, and it's worth noticing that Scripture presents it as a specific prophetic word for a specific moment, not a general rule for every conflict.

questions: Zedekiah said the king can do nothing to stop his officials. When have you used weakness as an excuse for not doing what you knew was right?
Ebed-melech was an outsider who spoke up when insiders stayed silent. Who are the people at the edges of your community who might see what others are missing?
Jeremiah's message was simple: surrender and live. Why do people so often choose a slow disaster over a humbling decision?
